title: It seemed right to him
hook: when someone wrongs you, remember he did what seemed right to him (Enchiridion 42)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body's business in passing, and real care for the mind. Your line was open the windows. What did you give your five minutes to? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, and in the half second before the horn, a whole story forms in your head about who they are. Selfish. Reckless. Probably like this all the time. Hardly anyone pauses to tell the other story: that from inside that car, the move made sense. Late for a shift. A kid crying in the back. A misjudged mirror. Or simply a belief that the lane was theirs. Section forty-two of the handbook asks you to tell that second story, every time. Today: it seemed right to him.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `A WHOLE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.` → `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does it or says it because he thinks it's right for him to. He can't act on what seems right to you. Only on what seems right to him. Second, who gets hurt. If what seemed right to him is wrong, he says, then he's the one harmed, because he's the one who was deceived. Epictetus gives an example from logic. If someone takes a true statement to be false, the statement isn't harmed. The person who got it wrong is. Third, the old root. This goes back to an idea often traced to Socrates, in Plato's dialogues: that nobody does wrong knowingly, believing it to be wrong. People act on what looks good to them, even when it isn't. The Stoics inherited that idea and built on it. So the person who wrongs you isn't a monster who chose evil. They're someone who saw it wrong. Fourth, the result. Starting from this, Epictetus says, you'll be gentle with the one who insults you. And he gives you a short phrase to say each time, only two words in his Greek, a little like a breath before reacting: it seemed so to him. That isn't an excuse for harm. You can still protect yourself, set a limit, even seek justice. What changes is the heat. You stop adding your own anger to their mistake. You see a person who judged badly, not an enemy. And that turns out to be lighter to carry.
screen: `HE DID WHAT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.` · `THE ONE DECEIVED IS THE ONE HARMED.` · `NO ONE DOES WRONG KNOWINGLY.` · `SAY IT EACH TIME: IT SEEMED SO TO HIM.` · then, large: `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who wronged you, not the worst, just someone. A sharp email. A broken promise. A rude driver. Now try, for a minute, to stand where they stood. What did it look like from inside their day? What did they believe was true, or fair, or necessary? You don't have to agree. Just look. Then say it quietly: it seemed right to him, or to her, or to them. Notice what happens to the heat. The bell holds the time.
Socrates. The thinker behind the idea that nobody does wrong knowingly; anyone who wrongs you acted on what seemed right to them, and their mistake is their harm. Today's word.
Your line: lighter to carry. Try to understand one wrongdoer today, from the inside of their day, before you decide what to do. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often remind themselves, when wronged, that the other person acted on what seemed right to them, which helps them respond without adding anger.

fork.setup: a coworker takes credit for your idea in a meeting. what phrase does Epictetus offer?
fork.reveal: he did what seemed right to him. if he judged wrongly, he's the one harmed. that frees you to respond without adding anger.

original.note: Greek: it seemed so to him, the two Greek words Enchiridion 42 asks you to say each time.

trapdoor: what you thought: just forgive and forget.
what it means: everyone acts on what seems right to them; if they judged wrongly, they carry the harm, and you can respond without anger.
what a scholar hears: an echo of the Socratic idea that no one does wrong knowingly, compressed into edoxen autō, it seemed so to him.

sources.ref: Plato, Protagoras 345d–e, 358c–d (no one does wrong willingly)

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): fixed a count error: the script called 'it seemed so to him' 'three words' (it is five in English and two in the Greek, ἔδοξεν αὐτῷ); teach, word, match, fork and original note corrected.

Enchiridion 42 paraphrased: when any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember he does or says it thinking it his duty; he cannot follow what seems right to you but what seems right to him; if he judges wrongly he is harmed, being deceived (the true conjunction example); so you will be mild to the one who reviles you, saying each time 'it seemed so to him'. Confirm.
Greek ἔδοξεν αὐτῷ as the closing phrase of Ench. 42: confirm wording and pronunciation.
Socratic 'no one does wrong willingly' (Protagoras 345d–e, 358c–d; also Gorgias): stated as 'often traced to Socrates'. Confirm references.
The script adds that the teaching doesn't require accepting harm (limits, justice). Confirm framing.
